title: Gikor
author: Hovhannes Tumanyan
short_summary: From a poor mountain village, Hambo takes his son Gikor to the city and apprentices him to the cloth merchant Bazaz Artem, hoping the boy will make something of himself and help the family. But in the city Gikor gets the samovar, the dishes, other people's boots and his master's beatings, while his heart stays in the village with his mother and the mountains. Made to stand in the cold outside the shop, he falls ill — and the story does not end the way his father hoped.
extended_summary:
Hambo, a poor peasant, takes his son Gikor to the city against his wife's tears: let the boy learn a trade, make something of himself and help the family. Gikor is apprenticed, unpaid, to the cloth merchant Bazaz Artem. As they part, his father gives him his advice: be honest, be grateful, and never touch what belongs to someone else.

In the city Gikor hardly works in the shop at all. He lights the samovar, washes the dishes, cleans the boots and runs the household errands. The master's mother, Dedi, is kind to him and shows him how things are done, but in that house Gikor always ends up in the wrong. One day, coming back from the market with his master, he innocently tells the mistress that the cherries were expensive so they did not buy any — and his master beats him savagely for it. Beatings and hunger, strangers and endless homesickness: that is Gikor's city life.

When the cold weather comes, he is stood at the shop door to call customers in. Gikor catches cold and falls ill. His master takes him to the city hospital, where he gets worse. Hambo comes to the city, but too late: Gikor dies. His father buries him and goes back to the village carrying the boy's clothes, so that his mother can weep over them.

questions.prompt: As they part, Hambo gives his son some advice. What does he tell Gikor?

options: Be honest, be grateful, never touch what is not yours
Say little, keep your eyes open, and save your money
Keep up your reading and write home every Sunday
If it goes badly, get up at once and come home

questions.explanation: The whole of the father's advice fits into three things: honesty, gratitude, and taking nothing. The bitter part is that Gikor keeps all three perfectly, and it does him no good at all — the story punishes not the boy's mistakes but his poverty.

questions.prompt: What work is Gikor actually given in his master's house?

options: Lighting the samovar, washing dishes, cleaning boots
Measuring cloth and showing goods to customers
Keeping the accounts and carrying his master's letters
Feeding the horses and loading the cart

questions.explanation: Gikor was brought to the city to learn a trade, and he barely sets foot in the shop. 'Apprenticeship' here turns out to mean domestic service: this is not a fairy tale but an account of what sending a poor village boy to the city actually meant.

questions.prompt: In the city Gikor works as an ___ in the shop of the merchant Bazaz Artem.
questions.explanation: The word does not mean a schoolboy here: it means an unpaid child worker learning a trade. The collision between the two senses of that one word is the story's bitterest irony.

questions.prompt: Back from the market, Gikor innocently tells the mistress that the cherries were expensive and they did not buy any. Why does his master beat him so savagely for it?

options: The boy has accidentally exposed him to his wife
The boy had eaten cherries at the market unasked
The boy had lost the rest of the market money
The boy had spoken to the mistress without leave

questions.explanation: Gikor has done nothing wrong; he has simply told the truth. The beating is not for a mistake but for a lie uncovered — and in that scene the child learns for the first time that in this house honesty is dangerous.

questions.prompt: Put the events of the story in the order they happen.

items: Hambo takes his son to the city against the mother's tears
Gikor is apprenticed to the merchant Bazaz Artem
In the house he is given the samovar and the dishes
After the story about the market, his master beats him
Standing in the cold by the shop, Gikor falls ill
Hambo goes back to the village with his son's clothes

questions.explanation: The story is a straight line downwards. Each step follows from the one before, and there is no point anywhere at which things could have turned upward: Tumanyan deliberately refuses to offer the reader any hope of rescue.

questions.prompt: Match each character to their part in the story.

right: The father who takes his son to the city to rise in life
The master in whose shop the boy was to learn a trade
The master's mother, kind to the boy and his teacher
The one who was against it, and weeps over the clothes

questions.explanation: Notice that the story has no real villain. The father wants what is best, the master is cruel but ordinary, Dedi is kind, the mother turns out to have been right. Tumanyan is not looking for someone to blame — he is showing an arrangement of the world in which this simply happens.

questions.prompt: Sort each moment by where it takes place.

options.label: A mother begs in tears not to take the boy
A father gives his advice before the road
The mountains and the house are left behind
A boy lights a samovar in someone else's kitchen
A boy stands at a shop door in the frost
A hospital bed becomes the last place of all

questions.explanation: The village gets only a couple of lines, and that is not an accident. Almost the whole of the story happens in the city, where Gikor lives in someone else's house, at someone else's work, and owns nothing anywhere.

questions.prompt: How does Gikor come to fall ill?

options: He stands in the frost calling customers in
He falls into the water on the way back from the market
He is given no food at all for a whole week
His master locks him in a cold cellar overnight

questions.explanation: He is put at the door to call people in, and he stands there for hours in the cold. Nobody wants him dead — he is simply used like a chair or a signboard, and that turns out to be enough.

questions.prompt: Hambo took his son to the city so that he would rise in life and help the family, and it ended in Gikor's death. Whose fault is what happened — the father's, the master's, or nobody's? Give your reasons.
questions.explanation: Any position can earn full marks. A strong answer rests on specific actions: the father did not listen to the mother, the master beat him and stood him in the frost, nobody called a doctor in time. The strongest answers notice that Hambo did it out of love and out of having no other choice — which is what makes the story heavier, not lighter.

questions.prompt: Imagine Gikor managed to send one letter home to his mother. What would he write in it, and what would he keep from her? Explain why.
questions.explanation: There is no single right answer. A strong answer gives both halves — what he would say and what he would leave out — and gives a reason for the silence: so his mother would not grieve, so his father would not be ashamed, so they would not fetch him back. It is the second half that shows the child has understood Gikor.

questions.prompt: Gikor dreams again and again of going back to his ___, although he cannot leave the shop.
questions.explanation: Homesickness is not decoration in this story; it is a symptom. Gikor asks for no food, no rest and no money — he wants to go back to one particular place, and that is precisely the thing he is never given.

questions.prompt: What does Hambo do at the end of the story?

options: Buries his son and takes his clothes back to the village
Demands money from the master for what has happened
Stays in the city to work in his son's place
Takes Bazaz Artem to court over the beatings

questions.explanation: He argues with nobody and asks nobody to answer for it: he buries his son and carries the clothes home so that the boy's mother can weep over them. That silence is Tumanyan's most terrible stroke — it does not even occur to Hambo that anyone could be held to account.
